# Moremi Ajasoro: Research Dossier

> **Traditional class:** mortal royal heroine and culture hero of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, subsequently heroized—and in some modern Ifẹ̀ descriptions deified—as the focus of shrines and the annual Edì festival. She is not securely attested as a divinity in an ancient written pantheon.
>
> **Earliest secure attestation:** Samuel Johnson’s *The History of the Yorubas*, completed in manuscript about 1897 but reconstructed after the original was lost and published in 1921, pp. 147–49, “The Legend of Moremi and Her Son.” This is the earliest presently identifiable, securely dated substantial written account. Johnson records an oral legend; he supplies no contemporary inscription, manuscript, archaeological object, or independent date for Moremi. The frequently repeated “twelfth-century queen” designation is a modern chronological inference from her association with the legendary king Ọ̀rànmíyàn, not a securely dated attestation.

## Evidentiary key

- **[EA] Securely attested early record:** a datable early documentation of the tradition—not proof that the narrated event occurred.
- **[LC] Later canonical elaboration:** a version that became influential through print, theatre, education, or palace sponsorship.
- **[RV] Regional or lineage variant.**
- **[LS] Learned or scholarly systematization/reconstruction.**
- **[F] Folklore or continuing oral tradition.**
- **[C] Cultic/ritual evidence:** observed ritual, shrine, office, or material commemoration.
- **[MR] Modern reception or reinterpretation.**
- **[MI] Modern invention or anachronistic claim.**
- **[Ø] No secure evidence located.**

---

## 1. Identification, Names and Epithets

Mọ̀rèmi—or, in the now common spelling, Mọ́remí—Àjàṣorò is the heroine of an Ilé-Ifẹ̀ tradition explaining the defeat of raiders called Igbo or Ugbo. In the best-known cycle she is a beautiful woman, usually the wife of Ọ̀rànmíyàn, who vows a costly offering to a stream power, allows herself to be captured, penetrates the enemy ruler’s household, discovers that the supposedly supernatural raiders wear combustible grass or raffia disguises, escapes, and gives Ifẹ̀ the knowledge needed to burn the disguises and defeat them. The stream then demands her only son, Elà or Olúorogbo. Her surrender of the child completes the paradigm of civic salvation through a mother’s unbearable sacrifice. **[EA: Johnson, c.1897/1921; LC: Ogumefu 1929; F/C: Walsh 1948 and later Edì documentation.]**

### Name and orthography

Attested modern forms include:

- **Moremi**, the undiacriticized colonial and English form used by Johnson in 1921 and M. I. Ogumefu in 1929. **[EA]**
- **Mọ́remí Àjàṣorò**, the most widespread contemporary standard-Yorùbá spelling. **[LC/MR]**
- **Mọ̀rèmi / Mọ́ rè mí**, proposed by linguist Ọládìpọ̀ Ajíbóyè after morphosyntactic and dialect inquiry. Ajíbóyè argues that the widespread high–mid–high pronunciation *Mọ́remí* is a perception or transcription error amplified by Dúró Ládipọ̀’s song, and that the name contracts *Ọmọ-ọ́ ń rè mí*, “the child/children please(s) me” or “having children delights me.” This is a **modern linguistic argument**, not an etymology demonstrably preserved from Moremi’s supposed era. **[LS: Ajíbóyè, published 2022/23.]**
- Popular websites sometimes derive the name from *mo rè mí* and gloss it as “I have suffered/endured.” No historical-linguistic demonstration for that interpretation was located; it should be treated as **[MI] popular etymology**, not established Yoruba philology.
- **Àjàṣorò / Àjànṣorò / Ajasoro / Ajansoro** are competing spellings or heard forms of the byname. A secure early explanation of its morphology was not found in Johnson or Ogumefu. Claims that it has one certain literal translation should therefore be treated cautiously. **[Ø/LS]**

### Titles and classifications

- **“Wife of one of the ancient heroes of Ile Ife, probably Oranmiyan”** is Johnson’s cautious formulation. He does not call her an Ooni’s reigning queen and signals uncertainty about the husband. **[EA: 1921]**
- **Wife of “a nobleman”** appears in Ogumefu’s version, which omits Ọ̀rànmíyàn. **[LC: 1929]**
- **Queen, princess, ayaba, Queen Moremi, heroine of Ifẹ̀, saviour/liberator of the Yoruba race**, and **mother of the Ifẹ̀ people** are later ritual, literary, educational, journalistic, and palace usages. **[LC/C/MR]**
- Descriptions of Moremi as an **òrìṣà**, “female deity,” or “goddess” reflect heroization in continuing Ifẹ̀ religion and modern classification. Her shrine and festival substantiate cultic treatment; they do not establish that she began as a primordial òrìṣà. **[C/LS]**
- No verified ancient patronymic, birth-name genealogy, indigenous written title, or contemporary royal inscription survives. **[Ø]**

### Identifications with other figures

Moremi is sometimes loosely compared with Delilah, Judith, Esther, Iphigenia, or the biblical God who sacrifices an only son. These are comparative interpretations, not traditional identifications. A doctoral study has suggested that Johnson’s Christian formation may have colored his presentation of the only-son sacrifice; this is a modern critical hypothesis, not evidence of derivation. **[LS]**

The names **Elà** and **Olúorogbo** can designate Moremi’s son in the legend, but Elà is also independently a divine or revelatory figure in Yoruba religious discourse. A recent Yoruba religious essay explicitly warns against conflating Moremi’s legendary Elà Olúorogbo with the separate divine Elà. **[F/LS]**

---

## 2. Earliest Attestation and Textual Corpus

### 2.1 Samuel Johnson: the earliest recoverable full record

Johnson finished his historical manuscript around 1897. The original was lost by a prospective publisher; after Johnson’s death, his brother Obadiah reconstructed it from surviving papers, and it appeared in 1921. Consequently the published text is the earliest secure documentary witness, while its exact relationship to the lost 1897 manuscript cannot be checked. **[EA]**

Johnson’s account supplies nearly the whole familiar narrative:

- Moremi is “probably” Ọ̀rànmíyàn’s wife.
- Her only son is “Ela or Olurogbo.”
- Igbo raiders repeatedly carry off valuables, women, and children.
- The Ifẹ̀ mistake them for gods or demigods.
- Moremi consults the “goddess of the river Esimirin” and promises her dearest possession.
- She intentionally becomes a captive.
- The Igbo ruler makes her a wife.
- She learns that the raiders’ terrible appearance comes from grass and bamboo-fibre coverings.
- She escapes and tells Ifẹ̀ to meet them with lighted torches.
- The raiders are defeated.
- After animals are rejected as payment, Moremi gives her son.
- The son is accepted among the gods, and the Ifẹ̀ promise to be Moremi’s children.
- Johnson associates the deed with continuing commemoration.

This is evidence that the cycle circulated by the late nineteenth century. It is not contemporary evidence for an event centuries earlier. **[EA]**

### 2.2 M. I. Ogumefu, *Yoruba Legends* (1929)

Ogumefu’s English collection presents “Moremi” as a folktale. The heroine is married simply to an Ifẹ̀ nobleman and her son is Ela. She promises the unnamed stream god “the richest sacrifice she could afford,” is captured and given to the Igbo king, learns the grass-and-bamboo disguise, escapes, and enables victory by fire. After she sacrifices Ela, he revives, makes a grass rope, climbs into heaven, and is expected someday to return. **[LC/F]**

This resurrection-and-ascension ending is absent from Johnson’s published account, where the child is received among the gods. It is a genuine variant, not something to harmonize away.

### 2.3 William Bascom’s field documentation (1937–38)

William Bascom’s Meko and Yoruba field notes reportedly record Moremi as Ọ̀rànmíyàn’s beautiful wife who allowed the Ugbo to capture her and learned their intimidation device. These field notes are important independent documentation of twentieth-century oral circulation but remain unpublished archival notes rather than a precolonial text. **[EA/F]**

### 2.4 Michael J. Walsh, “The Êdi Festival at Ile Ife” (1948)

Walsh’s article in *African Affairs* is the first readily identifiable extended published observation of the ritual complex. It documents the Edì festival as a major Ifẹ̀ ceremony and records songs and staged actions. Because Walsh wrote amid Yoruba–Igbo political tension, his language and equation of the legendary “Igbo” with contemporary Igbo require care. **[EA/C]**

### 2.5 Historical and art-historical syntheses

- Robert S. Smith’s *Kingdoms of the Yoruba* (1969; later editions) treats Moremi within traditions about Ifẹ̀’s early political formation. Smith regards the defeat of the Igbo and Moremi’s sacrifice as traditional history, while stressing the methodological difficulty of converting dynastic oral traditions into absolute chronology. **[LS]**
- Ade M. Obayemi’s “Ancient Ile-Ife: Another Cultural-Historical Reinterpretation” (1979) placed “Igbo” traditions within debates about autochthonous or earlier populations at Ifẹ̀. **[LS]**
- I. A. Akinjogbin and collaborators’ *The Cradle of a Race: Ife from the Beginning to 1980* (1992) integrated oral traditions, ritual institutions, and political history. **[LS]**
- Suzanne Preston Blier’s studies of Obalufon and ancient Ifẹ̀ reinterpret the story as memory of conflict between the Odùduwà-associated newcomers and earlier inhabitants associated with Obalufon. Blier notes the Moremi and Elà shrines, the Esinmirin/Omi-Igbo association, and related ritual dramas, but does not produce an inscription naming Moremi. **[LS]**
- Robin Law’s *The Oyo Empire* (1977) is relevant chiefly to the construction and political uses of Ọ̀rànmíyàn traditions. It does not independently verify Moremi. **[LS/Ø]**
- Jacob Egharevba’s *A Short History of Benin*—first Edo version in the early 1930s and revised English editions beginning in 1934—records Benin traditions about Prince Oranmiyan and the beginning of the Eweka dynasty. It supplies an important parallel tradition for Ọ̀rànmíyàn, but it does not independently attest Moremi or her marriage to him. **[EA for Benin’s Oranmiyan tradition; Ø for Moremi.]**
- J. D. Y. Peel’s work explains the nineteenth- and twentieth-century formation of a pan-Yoruba historical and religious field from local traditions, missionary writing, Christianity, Islam, and òrìṣà religion. Peel provides methodological context rather than a separate primary Moremi narrative. **[LS]**

### 2.6 Dramatic and literary corpus

- **Dúró Ládipọ̀, *Moremi***: written/produced in 1965; later circulated as a Yoruba photoplay around 1969–71. It transforms oral and ritual material into authored historical theatre. **[MR]**
- **Ulli Beier, *Moremi***: staged dramatic reworking, published in 1987; here Esinmerin becomes a voice for the dispossessed spirits/owners of the soil, and Olúorogbo’s death effects reconciliation between Odùduwà’s polity and prior inhabitants. **[MR/LS]**
- **Femi Osofisan, *Morountodun***: first performed in 1979 and published in 1982. Its protagonist Titubi deliberately models herself on Moremi when she infiltrates the 1968–69 Agbekoya peasant rebellion, but changes allegiance after encountering the rebels’ suffering. Osofisan turns Moremi from a straightforward patriot into a problem through which class power, betrayal, and revolutionary solidarity can be examined. **[MR]**
- **Segun Thomas Ajayi, *Moremi, the Courageous Queen***: a modern literary treatment that helped circulate the heroic national image. **[MR]**
- **2009 film *Moremi***: Abiodun Duro-Ladipo reportedly reprised Moremi, continuing the theatrical lineage on screen. **[MR]**
- **Queen Moremi: The Musical**: premiered at Terra Kulture, Lagos, on 21 December 2018 and returned in 2019. Produced through the House of Oduduwa/Queen Moremi Ajasoro Initiative orbit, it presents her as an ancestor of African women’s leadership and patriotism. **[MR]**

No ancient tablet, medieval manuscript, praise-poem manuscript, or early European traveler’s account naming Moremi was located. **[Ø]**

---

## 3. The Story

### 3.1 Status, household, and parentage

Nothing securely records Moremi’s parents, birthplace, birth, childhood, or death. Modern biographies that assign her a complete life-course are reconstructions. **[Ø/MI]**

Johnson calls her the wife of an ancient Ifẹ̀ hero, “probably Oranmiyan”; Ogumefu says only that a nobleman’s beautiful and virtuous wife was named Moremi. Later Ifẹ̀ and pan-Yoruba retellings promote her firmly to Ọ̀rànmíyàn’s queen. A modern Nigerian historical compilation notes another living variation: she is variously described as princess, queen, or commoner of the Òkèrèwè quarter. **[EA/RV]**

The widely repeated twelfth-century date is produced by joining her to chronologies assigned to Ọ̀rànmíyàn. Egharevba places Oranmiyan’s arrival in Benin at about 1170, but that is an internally reconstructed royal chronology, revised across editions, not an external date for Moremi. **[LS]**

### 3.2 The raiders

Johnson calls them “Igbos”; later writers often prefer **Ugbo**, partly to prevent an unsupported equation with the modern Igbo people of southeastern Nigeria. Ifẹ̀ traditions may use *igbo* in senses connected with forest, grove, or a named earlier population. Obayemi and Blier relate the traditions to sites such as Iwinrin/Igbo-Igbo grove and to Esinmirin as *Omi Igbo*, “Igbo water.” **[EA/LS]**

In the Ifẹ̀ account, the raiders abduct people and goods while disguised as terrifying beings. The Ifẹ̀ suppose them to be gods, demigods, spirits, or *egúngún*. Later versions make the costumes explicitly raffia. **[EA/F/LC]**

A political-historical reading sees the story as compressed memory of conflict between an Odùduwà-linked ruling formation and autochthonous groups. This interpretation is plausible because local cults, place-names, and counter-traditions preserve an “earlier inhabitants” theme, but archaeology has not identified Moremi, her mission, or a burnable-costume battle. **[LS]**

### 3.3 The vow

Johnson names the river as Esimirin and its power as a goddess. Ogumefu leaves the stream and deity unnamed. Later accounts use **Esinmirin, Esimirin, Esinminrin**, or **Esinmerin** and variously describe the recipient as goddess, god, river spirit, or the river itself. **[EA/RV]**

Johnson says Moremi promises her dearest possession; Ogumefu says the richest sacrifice she could afford. Some later retellings say she explicitly promises anything asked. Others say from the outset that she pledges Olúorogbo. The last formulation removes the shock and failed substitution that structure the older printed narratives. **[EA/LC/RV]**

### 3.4 Capture and sexual-political danger

Moremi deliberately remains behind or places herself where capture is likely. The raiders carry her away as enslaved booty. Johnson and Ogumefu say her beauty brings her to the enemy ruler, who takes her as a wife or concubine/slave-wife. Later decorous versions sometimes soften this into mere residence at court.

The story therefore entails enslavement, coerced incorporation into an enemy ruler’s household, and implied sexual availability under captivity. Neither Johnson nor Ogumefu narrates rape explicitly; calling the episode consensual romance would be equally unsupported. **[EA]**

In elaborated versions she wins the king’s confidence, sometimes intoxicates him with palm wine, and obtains his secret. The palm-wine stratagem is not in Johnson or Ogumefu and belongs to later oral/literary narration. **[F/LC]**

### 3.5 The secret and return

The early printed versions agree that the raiders are ordinary human beings wearing dry grass, bamboo fibre, or comparable vegetable coverings. Moremi escapes and teaches Ifẹ̀ to confront them with torches. Their supposed supernatural invulnerability is destroyed by knowledge: the masks burn. **[EA]**

Some modern accounts say Moremi herself led the battle. Johnson and Ogumefu say she supplied the decisive intelligence and stratagem; they do not describe her commanding troops. “Warrior queen leading an army” is therefore a modern expansion unless tied to a named performance or retelling. **[MI/MR]**

### 3.6 The sacrifice of Elà/Olúorogbo

Johnson’s son is “Ela or Olurogbo”; Ogumefu calls him Ela; later tradition favors **Elà Olúorogbo** or **Oluorogbo**. Johnson says Moremi first presents animals, which the river rejects, and finally yields the boy. The episode is human sacrifice and filicide within the story, however reverently it is framed. **[EA]**

Outcomes differ:

- **Johnson:** the child dies/is sacrificed and is “received amongst the gods”; Ifẹ̀’s inhabitants promise to become Moremi’s children. **[EA: 1921]**
- **Ogumefu:** Ela is only half-dead, revives after the crowd leaves, makes a grass rope, climbs to heaven, and will return. **[LC/RV: 1929]**
- **Later shrine tradition:** Moremi and Olúorogbo have distinct shrines, encouraging treatment of the son as a heroized or divine being. **[C]**
- **Beier’s dramatic version:** the sacrifice reconciles Odùduwà’s polity with the spirits of the dispossessed landowners; Olúorogbo becomes their link. **[MR]**
- **Popular retellings:** often say simply that she “sacrificed her only son,” omitting resurrection, deification, substitutions, or political reconciliation. **[LC/MR]**

No independent evidence verifies an actual child’s killing. Ritual commemoration demonstrates belief and cultural memory, not the historicity of the sacrifice. **[Ø]**

### 3.7 Death, body, and tomb

No early source describes Moremi’s death, burial, bones, relics, or a tomb. The Ifẹ̀ material documents a shrine and well/stream, not an archaeologically identified grave. Websites saying the Edì festival began “shortly after her death” turn an undated aetiology into chronology. **[Ø/MI]**

## 4. Relations with Gods and Other Heroes

### Competing relational schemes

| Relation | Version | Source and date | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Husband | An unnamed nobleman | Ogumefu, 1929 | LC/RV |
| Husband | An ancient Ifẹ̀ hero, “probably Oranmiyan” | Johnson, c.1897/1921 | EA |
| Husband | Ọ̀rànmíyàn, king/prince of Ifẹ̀ and founder linked with Oyo and Benin | Later Ifẹ̀ tradition; Bascom notes, 1937–38; twentieth-century drama and scholarship | F/LC/LS |
| Child | Elà | Johnson 1921; Ogumefu 1929 | EA/LC |
| Child | Olurogbo/Olúorogbo | Johnson 1921 and later shrine tradition | EA/C |
| Child | Elà Olúorogbo as one person | Modern synthesis | LC/LS |
| Divine helper/creditor | Goddess of River Esimirin | Johnson 1921 | EA |
| Divine helper/creditor | Unnamed stream god | Ogumefu 1929 | LC/RV |
| Captor/second husband | Unnamed Igbo/Ugbo king | Johnson 1921; Ogumefu 1929 | EA/LC |
| Political predecessor/enemy | Obalufon II or forces representing earlier inhabitants | Blier’s art-historical reconstruction from Ifẹ̀ traditions | LS |
| Father-in-law by later genealogy | Odùduwà, father of Ọ̀rànmíyàn | Later harmonized royal genealogy | LC/LS |

No secure source supplies Moremi with siblings, daughters, additional sons, or a named human father or mother. **[Ø]**

### Every documented interaction with another named divine being or hero

- **Ọ̀rànmíyàn / Ọranyan / Oranmiyan** — Moremi is cautiously called “probably” his wife by Johnson; Bascom’s 1937–38 notes and later Ifẹ̀ accounts make the marriage definite. Johnson does not give the husband an active role in her mission. **Source:** Johnson, c.1897/1921; Bascom field notes, 1937–38. **Tier:** EA/F.

- **Elà** — Her only son and the eventual demanded sacrifice; in Ogumefu he revives and ascends. **Source:** Johnson 1921; Ogumefu 1929. **Tier:** EA/LC/RV.

- **Olúorogbo / Olurogbo** — Alternate or compound name of the son sacrificed to fulfill Moremi’s vow; later the focus of a distinct Ifẹ̀ shrine. **Source:** Johnson 1921; *Ife Shrines* 1969; later festival tradition. **Tier:** EA/C.

- **Esimirin / Esinmirin / Esinmerin** — River power to whom Moremi vows an offering; grants or enables success and subsequently demands her dearest possession/son. **Source:** Johnson 1921; later Ifẹ̀ shrine and festival documentation. **Tier:** EA/C.

- **Obalufon II** — In Blier’s reconstruction, Moremi is captured by forces associated with Obalufon and discovers that the supposed spirits are earlier Ifẹ̀ inhabitants. This identification is not made by Johnson or Ogumefu. **Source:** Blier, 1985 and later work. **Tier:** LS.

- **Odùduwà / Odudua** — No early narrative scene directly joins him to Moremi. He becomes her father-in-law only through the later definitive marriage to his son Ọ̀rànmíyàn; Beier’s play makes Moremi’s crisis a consequence of Odùduwà’s conquest and displacement of land spirits. **Source:** later royal genealogy; Beier, 1987. **Tier:** LC/MR.

- **Ajagemo** — No direct encounter with Moremi is documented. Ajagemo appears in related Ifẹ̀ ritual as a polyvalent representation of autochthonous people, Ọbàtálá, and Obalufon II; joining the figure to Moremi as a personal companion would exceed the evidence. **Source:** Ifẹ̀ ritual interpreted by Blier. **Tier:** C/LS/Ø for direct interaction.

- **Ọbàtálá** — No early Moremi narrative records a meeting. The connection is indirect through the symbolism of related Ifẹ̀ ritual drama. **Source:** Blier’s interpretation. **Tier:** LS/Ø for direct interaction.

- **Olunwi** — A figure in the associated ritual opposition who represents Odùduwà/Ọ̀rànmíyàn’s side; no text examined gives a personal encounter with Moremi. **Source:** ritual account interpreted by Blier. **Tier:** C/LS/Ø.

- **Other named òrìṣà or heroes:** no securely sourced interaction with Ọ̀ṣun, Yemoja, Ògún, Ṣàngó, Èṣù, Ọ̀rúnmìlà, or Olókun was located in the early Moremi accounts. Appearances of such deities in modern plays are dramaturgical additions unless separately sourced. **[Ø]**

---

## 5. Cult, Shrine, Well, and Ritual

### Moremi shrine and Esinmirin

A Moremi shrine and the Esinminrin stream were documented in the illustrated survey *Ife Shrines* (1969), which gives them a dedicated chapter. A separate Olúorogbo shrine is also catalogued. These are material and institutional evidence for hero cult in twentieth-century Ifẹ̀, although they are not securely dated archaeologically to Moremi’s supposed era. **[C]**

Smithsonian archival photography records the “Well of Moremi” shrine in the garden of the Ooni’s palace. The photograph confirms a named commemorative site; it does not identify a tomb or ancient construction date. **[C]**

Modern sources identify a hereditary or chiefly custodian, the **Owa Yekere/Oba Isoro**, and refer to the Yekere as Moremi’s indigenous family or shrine community. Those offices substantiate continuing institutional custody, but modern title-holders’ claims about remote antiquity remain oral/ritual claims. **[C/F]**

### The Edì festival

Walsh’s 1948 article is the key early published ethnographic description. Later research describes Edì as:

- an annual commemoration and ritual reenactment of the Ugbo crisis, Moremi’s action, and communal victory;
- a complex including palace, shrine, priestly, costumed, musical, gendered, and sometimes sexually explicit or license-granting performances;
- a festival in which the *opa*, a costumed or emblematic form associated with Moremi, appears;
- a rite at which women may seek fertility;
- a festival whose concluding ritual is called **Ìgbárùbì-Edì** in modern scholarship;
- a ritual whose components cannot be reduced to a simple historical pageant, since the festival also negotiates purity, fertility, social inversion, autochthony, kingship, and relations among quarters. **[C/LS]**

An Edì festival is also observed at Ipetumodu and is locally treated as evidence of historical relations with Ifẹ̀. Its practices include a shrine-held *opa* under a chief priest’s custody. This is a regional extension, not proof that every component originated simultaneously. **[RV/C]**

### Archaeology

No excavated object bearing Moremi’s name has been reported. Ifẹ̀ archaeology securely establishes a major medieval urban, artistic, industrial, and ritual center, with its renowned terracottas, copper-alloy heads, glassworking, pavements, and sacred sites. It supplies the historical environment in which later traditions place Moremi but does not verify her individual existence. **[Ø/LS]**

The Oranmiyan staff, **Ọ̀pá Ọ̀rànmíyàn**, is a tall stone monolith at Ifẹ̀ traditionally linked to her supposed husband. Its existence demonstrates the material commemoration of Ọ̀rànmíyàn, not his marriage to Moremi. **[C/Ø]**

### Statue of 2016

On 21–22 November 2016, the Ooni of Ifẹ̀, Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi Ojaja II, unveiled a 42-foot/12.8-metre statue within the palace complex. Often called the **Moremi Statue of Liberty**, it monumentalizes Moremi as Yoruba liberator and has been promoted as a major tourist landmark. It is modern commemorative art, not an ancient cult image. **[MR]**

The work replaced neither the evidentiary gap nor the older shrine; it represents palace-sponsored twenty-first-century heritage production. Claims that it was then Nigeria’s tallest statue were widely made, but rankings are time-sensitive and do not affect its religious-historical significance.

### Ugbo counter-monument

After the Ifẹ̀ unveiling, the Olugbo of Ugbo, Oba Frederick Obateru Akinruntan, unveiled a contrasting statue at Ode-Ugbo portraying Moremi kneeling and asking forgiveness. He declared her not a liberator but a **traitor**: a woman married into the Ugbo ruler’s house who betrayed Ugbo military secrets to Odùduwà’s people. **[RV/MR]**

This is the most explicit contemporary counter-memory. It preserves the same structural acts—capture/marriage, acquisition of the disguise secret, disclosure to Ifẹ̀—but reverses their ethics. Ifẹ̀’s saviour becomes Ugbo’s betrayer. Neither monumental version independently proves the underlying war; together they demonstrate an active politics of memory and autochthony.

---

## 6. Historical Evolution of the Figure

### Undated oral and ritual formation

The cycle was oral before its first surviving written record. The age of particular episodes cannot be calculated merely from the story’s placement in the time of Ọ̀rànmíyàn. The fire stratagem, sacrifice, child’s heavenly fate, and “all Ifẹ̀ are her children” may have circulated in changing combinations. **[F/Ø]**

### Late nineteenth century–1921: historical codification

Johnson incorporated the legend into a comprehensive Yoruba history. His work helped move a local or regional narrative into a pan-Yoruba printed historical framework. His cautious “probably Oranmiyan” shows that the marriage was not yet presented to him as entirely fixed. **[EA/LS]**

### 1929: folktale canon

Ogumefu detached the heroine from named royal genealogy, rendered the story as compact English folklore, and added the striking resurrection, grass-rope ascension, and promised return of Ela. **[LC]**

### 1930s–1940s: ethnographic and ritual record

Bascom collected oral material in 1937–38; Walsh documented Edì in 1948. These records show that Moremi was not merely a literary creation of Johnson: her cycle existed in oral and ritual contexts. They still do not allow the festival’s foundation to be dated. **[EA/C]**

### 1960s–1980s: postcolonial theatre and historical reconstruction

Dúró Ládipọ̀’s 1965 play established Moremi as a major modern Nigerian stage heroine. Post-independence historians used the tradition to examine Ifẹ̀ state formation, autochthony, dynastic ideology, and Yoruba unity. Beier and Osofisan then destabilized triumphalist readings: Beier foregrounded displaced land spirits, while Osofisan used Moremi’s infiltration as the template for Titubi’s encounter with class rebellion. **[MR/LS]**

### 1990s–2000s: heritage and gender icon

Academic, educational, and popular discourse increasingly presented Moremi as proof of indigenous African female leadership. Schools and women’s residence halls, including Moremi Hall at Obafemi Awolowo University and a hall at the University of Lagos, bear her name. These commemorations universalized her beyond the ritual confines of Ifẹ̀. **[MR]**

### 2010s–present: palace-sponsored global icon

The 2016 monument, Queen Moremi cultural pageants, leadership awards, scholarships, anti-trafficking campaigns, women’s entrepreneurship programs, the 2018–19 musical, and digital storytelling recast Moremi as a global Black women’s empowerment figure. **[MR]**

This modern formulation often calls her a feminist who lived “over 1,700 years ago” or a precisely dated twelfth-century queen. The feminist interpretation is a legitimate modern reception; the numerical antiquity is unsupported by the available documentary record. **[MR/MI]**

---

## 7. Modern Reception and Reinvention

### Theatre and film

Dúró Ládipọ̀’s *Moremi* made the story part of the Yoruba travelling-theatre repertoire. The work’s songs helped standardize how later audiences pronounced and remembered the heroine’s name. Abiodun Duro-Ladipo’s association with the role and reported return in the 2009 film linked stage, family repertory, television, and Nollywood-era heritage performance. **[MR]**

Osofisan’s *Morountodun* is the most important critical reinvention. Titubi enters the peasants’ camp expecting to reproduce Moremi’s patriotic betrayal of an enemy. She instead discovers that the state’s “enemy” consists of exploited farmers and turns against her own class. The play asks who has the authority to label another population monstrous and whether civic heroism can serve ruling-class violence. **[MR]**

*Queen Moremi: The Musical* premiered in Lagos in December 2018 and returned at Easter 2019. Its producers explicitly connected Moremi with African feminism, cultural pride, and women’s leadership. This claim belongs to contemporary political theatre, not to a recoverable medieval vocabulary of feminism. **[MR]**

### Public sculpture and visual representation

Before the 2016 monument, sculptures existed at the Ooni’s palace and at Moremi Hall, Obafemi Awolowo University; a 2010 comparative art study treated them as embodiments of Yoruba aesthetics. The 42-foot palace statue transformed the heroine into monumental public heritage. **[MR]**

The rival Ugbo statue is equally significant: public sculpture became an argument about conquest, land, betrayal, and whose account controls Yoruba origins. **[RV/MR]**

### Women’s associations and empowerment

The House of Oduduwa’s **Queen Moremi Ajasoro Initiative**, launched under Ooni Ogunwusi, sponsors:

- cultural and leadership pageants for young women;
- Queen Moremi Leadership Awards;
- education and scholarships;
- entrepreneurship and small-business support;
- campaigns against trafficking of women;
- mentoring and cultural education;
- “Queen Riders,” a commercial mobility/empowerment partnership;
- assistance to women of the Yekere shrine community.

The organization calls Moremi a model of leadership, selflessness, elegance, courage, and Black women’s empowerment. These are documented modern institutional uses of the legend. **[MR]**

The figure also functions more broadly in Nigerian women’s-history writing beside Amina of Zazzau, Efunsetan Aniwura, Madam Tinubu, and twentieth-century women activists. Such lists create a long genealogy of female public authority; they should not be mistaken for evidence that all the figures are equally documented or contemporaneous. **[MR/LS]**

### Nationalism and ethnicity

Moremi has been used as:

- an emblem of pan-Yoruba unity and Ifẹ̀’s primacy;
- a nationalist female counterpart to male dynastic founders;
- proof that female leadership is indigenous rather than imported;
- a palace and tourism brand;
- a symbol through which Ifẹ̀ claims liberation and Ugbo claims betrayal.

Careless modern retellings equate the legendary Igbo/Ugbo with the modern southeastern Igbo ethnic nation. The early spelling permits the confusion, but Ifẹ̀ local-history scholarship usually treats the attackers as a local Ugbo/“forest” or autochthonous population. Deploying the legend against contemporary Igbo people is historically unsupported. **[MI/political misuse]**

No documented extremist movement centered on Moremi was found. Ethnic polemic and palace rivalry are documented; an organized extremist cult is not. **[Ø]**

### Commercial and digital uses

The name now appears in pageants, awards, schools, halls, tourism promotion, fashion and heritage initiatives, film projects, illustrated retellings, social media, and businesses. AI-style mythology databases increasingly assign her standardized “domains,” “symbols,” and epithets such as “Queen of Sacrifice.” Those taxonomies are modern inventions unless tied to an identifiable ritual source. **[MI/MR]**

A purported work titled *Moremi: A Legend of Our Time* by Wole Soyinka, dated 1996, circulates on automated name websites. No reliable bibliographic evidence for such a Soyinka play was found. It should be treated as fabricated metadata. **[MI]**

---

## 8. Historiography and Scholarly Debate

### Was Moremi historical?

The evidence allows three propositions of different strength:

1. By the late nineteenth century, a developed Moremi legend existed and was understood as part of Ifẹ̀’s ancient history. **Secure.**
2. By the 1930s–40s it circulated orally and was embedded in shrine and festival practice. **Secure.**
3. A single datable woman performed all the narrated deeds in the twelfth century. **Unverified.**

Historians including Smith, Obayemi, Akinjogbin, and Blier have treated the tradition as evidence for historical processes—migration, dynastic change, conflict with earlier populations, ritual accommodation—without thereby proving every narrative detail. **[LS]**

### Who were the Igbo/Ugbo?

The principal positions are:

- **Johnson/Ogumefu wording:** a people called Igbos, appearing superhuman because of disguise. **[EA]**
- **Modern Ifẹ̀ local-historical interpretation:** Ugbo or forest-associated enemies, not the modern southeastern Igbo nation. **[F/LS]**
- **Autochthony interpretation:** descendants or representatives of populations displaced or subordinated by Odùduwà’s incoming order. **[LS]**
- **Ugbo royal counter-tradition:** the Ugbo were the legitimate earlier inhabitants, and Moremi betrayed them after entering their ruler’s household. **[RV]**
- **Obalufon reconstruction:** the opponents were forces associated with Obalufon II and the old population; the legend encodes political restoration and accommodation. **[LS]**

These theories overlap but are not identical. Archaeology establishes multiple occupation phases and a complex medieval city, not the ethnic identity of Moremi’s raiders.

### Was the disguise raffia?

Johnson says grass and bamboo fibre; Ogumefu says grass and bamboo-fibre mantles. Raffia is the standard later specification. The combustible vegetal disguise is therefore early in the written record, while the exact botany is unstable. **[EA/LC]**

### What happened to Olúorogbo?

Death/deification, partial death followed by ascension, promised return, and ritual survival as a shrine figure are all attested. Any version that reports only execution suppresses a major variant. **[EA/RV/C]**

### Is Moremi an òrìṣà?

The shrine, festival, priestly custody, petitions for fertility, and modern description as a deity establish religious veneration. But Johnson presents her as human and distinguishes her from the river goddess. The most precise classification is **heroized human with local cult**, sometimes called an òrìṣà in present discourse. **[EA/C]**

### Is Edì a straightforward historical reenactment?

No. It remembers Moremi and Ugbo conflict, but ethnographic work also shows ritual license, fertility concerns, purification, kingship, gender performance, and relations between autochthonous and dynastic constituencies. Calling it merely a “Moremi pageant” understates its ritual complexity. **[C/LS]**

### The problem of Johnson

Johnson is indispensable but not transparent. He was an Oyo-based Anglican intellectual constructing a connected Yoruba past in a period when “Yoruba” identity was itself being enlarged and standardized. His manuscript’s loss and fraternal reconstruction complicate textual history. Christian narrative patterns may have influenced presentation, but resemblance between Olúorogbo and Christ cannot demonstrate borrowing by itself. **[LS]**

### The limits of Bascom, Law, Peel, and Egharevba

- Bascom confirms twentieth-century oral circulation but not medieval fact.
- Law helps analyze Ọ̀rànmíyàn and Oyo dynastic ideology but offers no independent Moremi witness.
- Peel explains the historical making of Yoruba religious and ethnic consciousness rather than authenticating Moremi.
- Egharevba confirms that Benin had an Oranmiyan dynastic tradition, but does not confirm Moremi as Oranmiyan’s wife.

Using any of these authors as if they independently dated Moremi is circular. **[LS]**

### State of the material record

Known evidence includes:

- Johnson’s reconstructed published text;
- Ogumefu’s printed folktale;
- Bascom’s archival field notes;
- Walsh’s ethnographic festival account;
- shrines, well/stream, priestly offices, and festival performance;
- modern statues, photographs, plays, films, recordings, and institutional archives.

Missing evidence includes:

- contemporary inscription or manuscript;
- securely identified portrait;
- excavated grave or relic;
- ancient object bearing her name;
- independent date for the vow, war, sacrifice, shrine foundation, or first Edì festival.

---

## 9. Chronology of Attestation and Cultic History

| Date | Attestation or development | Evidence status |
|---|---|---|
| Medieval period, often assigned to the 12th–14th centuries | Proposed historical setting through association with Ọ̀rànmíyàn and ancient Ifẹ̀ political change | LS; no contemporary Moremi evidence |
| c. 1170 | Egharevba’s reconstructed date for Oranmiyan’s coming to Benin | Later Benin royal chronology; does not date Moremi |
| c. 1897 | Samuel Johnson completes the lost manuscript of *The History of the Yorubas* | Earliest datable composition known to have contained the legend, inferred from the 1921 reconstruction |
| 1921 | Johnson’s “The Legend of Moremi and Her Son” published | Earliest secure substantial written attestation |
| 1929 | M. I. Ogumefu publishes “Moremi” in *Yoruba Legends* | Early literary folklore witness; contains Ela’s revival and ascent |
| 1934 onward | Egharevba’s Benin history publishes Oranmiyan traditions | Contextual parallel only |
| 1937–38 | William Bascom records Moremi traditions in Yoruba field notes | Archival oral-history witness |
| 1948 | Michael J. Walsh publishes “The Êdi Festival at Ile Ife” | First major published ritual description |
| 1965 | Dúró Ládipọ̀ produces/writes *Moremi* | Major postcolonial stage canonization |
| 1969 | *Ife Shrines* catalogs Moremi shrine, Esinminrin stream, and Olúorogbo shrine | Material/cultic documentation |
| c. 1969–71 | Ládipọ̀’s *Moremi* circulates in Yoruba photoplay form | Popular visual-theatrical dissemination |
| 1979 | Osofisan’s *Morountodun* first performed | Radical class-conscious reinterpretation |
| 1979 | Obayemi publishes cultural-historical reinterpretation of ancient Ifẹ̀ | Autochthony debate |
| 1982 | *Morountodun and Other Plays* published | Canonical modern literary reception |
| 1985 and later | Blier connects Moremi, Obalufon, shrines, and ritual politics | Art-historical reconstruction |
| 1987 | Beier’s *Moremi* version published | Reconciliation-with-land-spirits reinterpretation |
| 1992 | Akinjogbin et al., *The Cradle of a Race* | Ifẹ̀-centered historical synthesis |
| 2009 | Modern film *Moremi* and scholarly study of palace/university statues | Screen and sculptural reception |
| November 2016 | 42-foot Moremi statue unveiled in the Ooni’s palace | Palace-sponsored monumental commemoration |
| 2017–18 | Ugbo ruler unveils counter-statue portraying Moremi as traitor | Regional counter-memory |
| 21 Dec. 2018–2 Jan. 2019 | *Queen Moremi: The Musical* premieres at Terra Kulture | Modern theatrical heritage |
| 2019 | Musical returns; QMA Initiative expands pageantry and empowerment work | Institutionalized reception |
| 2020s | Continuing Edì festivals, QMA awards, scholarships, anti-trafficking and entrepreneurship programs | Living ritual and civic commemoration |
| 2022/23 | Ajíbóyè publishes linguistic argument for *Mọ̀rèmi / Mọ́ rè mí* | Modern onomastic reassessment |
| 2026 | Moremi remains active in Ifẹ̀ festival, palace, tourism, women’s leadership, theatre, and digital culture | Present reception; not new ancient evidence |

- Walsh, Michael J. “The Êdi Festival at Ile Ife.” *African Affairs* 47.189 (1948): 231–38.
- Egharevba, Jacob U. *A Short History of Benin*. First English edition 1934; 4th ed., Ibadan University Press, 1968.
- Eluyemi, Omotoso. *Ife Shrines*. University of Ife, 1969.

### Historical, archaeological, religious, and art-historical studies

- Smith, Robert S. *Kingdoms of the Yoruba*. London: Methuen, 1969; revised editions.
- Law, Robin. *The Oyo Empire, c. 1600–c. 1836*. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1977.
- Obayemi, Ade M. “Ancient Ile-Ife: Another Cultural-Historical Reinterpretation.” 1979.
- Blier, Suzanne Preston. “Obalufon Arts at Ife.” *Art Bulletin* 67.3 (1985): 383–401.

- Akinjogbin, I. A., ed. *The Cradle of a Race: Ife from the Beginning to 1980*. Port Harcourt: Sunray, 1992.

- Ajíbóyè, Ọládìpọ̀. “Mọ́remí or Mọ̀rèmi: An Investigation into the Perception Error of a Deified Woman in Ilé-Ifẹ̀.” *Yoruba Studies Review*.
- Fasan, Rotimi. “Arugba: Superwoman, Power and Agency.” Study of Osofisan’s revision of Moremi.
- Adeyemi, Mercy Ayọ̀ Fasehun, and Ìlúfóyè Fáwọlé Òjó. “Àfihàn Akitiyan Akọnibìnrin Mọrèmi Àjàṣorò…” *Njinga & Sepé*, 2026.

### Literary and performance sources

- Ládipọ̀, Dúró. *Moremi*. First produced/written 1965.
- Osofisan, Femi. *Morountodun and Other Plays*. Longman Nigeria, 1982; first performance 1979.
- Beier, Ulli. *Moremi*. Published dramatic version, 1987.
- *Queen Moremi: The Musical*. Terra Kulture, Lagos, 2018–19.
- House of Oduduwa/Queen Moremi Ajasoro Initiative publications and programs, 2010s–present.

### Evidentiary conclusion

Moremi’s dossier is unusually rich in ritual survival and modern reinvention but thin in early documentation. The historical minimum is not “a twelfth-century queen whose biography is known.” It is that, by the late nineteenth century, Yoruba narrators possessed an elaborate Ifẹ̀ legend about a woman who defeated terrifying raiders through capture, intelligence, and disclosure, then paid for communal salvation with her only son; by the mid-twentieth century the story was demonstrably embedded in shrines and Edì ritual. The marriage to Ọ̀rànmíyàn, the identity of the Ugbo, the son’s fate, Moremi’s status as queen or commoner, and the meaning and pronunciation of her name remain variant or debated. Those disagreements are not defects in the record: they are the record.
